concepts.name: Simple Majority: Definition and Constitutional Basis
key_dimensions: Definition: majority of members present and voting (not total membership)
Distinguished from Absolute Majority — UPSC trap on 'present and voting' vs 'total strength'
Used for ordinary legislation under Article 245 — most common legislative decisions
Quorum requirements under Article 100 as a prerequisite to simple majority voting

concepts.name: Absolute Majority: Concept and Application
key_dimensions: Definition: more than 50% of total membership of the House (not just present and voting)
Not explicitly mentioned in Constitution but used in political/academic discourse — UPSC trap
Relevant in context of government formation: a party needs majority of total Lok Sabha strength (273+)
Contrast with Simple Majority — critical differentiation often tested

concepts.name: Effective Majority: Meaning and Specific Use Cases
key_dimensions: Definition: more than 50% of effective strength (total membership minus vacancies)
Used for removal of Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha (Article 94) and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Article 90)
UPSC trap: Speaker removal requires Special Majority (Article 93) but Deputy Speaker removal uses Effective Majority
Significance of 'vacancies' — effective strength can be lower than total sanctioned strength

concepts.name: Special Majority under Article 368: Constitutional Amendment
key_dimensions: Requires 2/3rd majority of members present and voting + majority of total membership of each House
Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously — UPSC trap on 'AND' not 'OR'
No joint sitting provision for constitutional amendments — each House must independently pass
Applies to most constitutional amendments; distinguished from amendments also requiring state ratification

concepts.name: Special Majority with State Ratification (Article 368 Proviso)
key_dimensions: Additional requirement: ratification by at least half of the state legislatures by simple majority
Applies to specific provisions: federal features — Article 54, 55, 73, 162, Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, 7th Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, Article 368 itself
State legislature ratification uses Simple Majority — UPSC trap on majority type at state level
No time limit prescribed for state ratification — constitutional gap

concepts.name: Special Majority for Removal of Constitutional Functionaries
key_dimensions: Removal of Supreme Court/High Court Judges (Articles 124, 217): Special Majority — 2/3rd present and voting + majority of total membership
Removal of CAG, CEC, Chairman UPSC uses same procedure as Supreme Court Judge removal
Removal of Vice President (Article 67): Simple Majority in Rajya Sabha + agreement of Lok Sabha — UPSC trap
Removal of President (Article 61): 2/3rd of total membership of each House — stricter than Article 368 Special Majority

concepts.name: Presidential Impeachment Majority: A Unique Special Majority
key_dimensions: Article 61: requires 2/3rd of the TOTAL membership of each House (not just present and voting) — most stringent majority
Distinct from Article 368 Special Majority — UPSC high-value trap
Joint sitting NOT applicable for impeachment — each House must pass separately
Initiated in either House — unlike money bill which originates only in Lok Sabha

concepts.name: Majority Required for No-Confidence Motion
key_dimensions: Simple Majority (majority of members present and voting) in Lok Sabha only
No-confidence motion not applicable to Rajya Sabha — UPSC trap on applicability
Minimum 50 members must support the notice for admission — not the passage
Defeat of no-confidence motion vs. passage: government must resign only on passage, not on admission

concepts.name: Majority for Speaker and Deputy Speaker Election and Removal
key_dimensions: Election of Speaker/Deputy Speaker: Simple Majority (Article 93)
Removal of Speaker: Special Majority — effective majority of total membership + 14 days prior notice (Article 94) — UPSC trap: notice requirement
Removal of Deputy Speaker: Effective Majority with 14 days prior notice (Article 94)
During removal resolution discussion, Speaker can be present and even vote — unique privilege

concepts.name: Majority for National Emergency Proclamation and Revocation
key_dimensions: Approval of National Emergency (Article 352): Special Majority — 2/3rd of members present and voting + majority of total membership, within one month
Revocation by Lok Sabha: Simple Majority via special sitting demanded by 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members
UPSC trap: Continuation requires re-approval every six months by Special Majority
Proclamation by Cabinet in writing — not just President's satisfaction

concepts.name: Majority Requirements for President's Rule (Article 356) and Financial Emergency
key_dimensions: President's Rule approval: Simple Majority within 2 months; continuation every 6 months by Simple Majority — UPSC trap: NOT Special Majority
Financial Emergency (Article 360): Simple Majority for approval and continuation — least stringent among emergency provisions
Contrast: National Emergency requires Special Majority for continuance but President's Rule requires only Simple Majority
Revocation of President's Rule: President can revoke without Parliament approval — no majority needed

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law Majority Requirements (Tenth Schedule)
key_dimensions: Merger exemption: requires 2/3rd of the legislature party (not political party) to merge — UPSC trap on 'legislature party' vs 'political party'
Decision by Speaker/Chairman — not by the House itself, hence no 'majority' of House needed
91st Amendment abolished the split provision (1/3rd split) — only merger exemption survives
Kihoto Hollohan case: Speaker's decision subject to judicial review — not final

concepts.name: Majority for Creation/Abolition of Legislative Councils (Article 169)
key_dimensions: Resolution by State Legislative Assembly: Special Majority — 2/3rd of members present and voting + majority of total membership
Parliament then passes an ordinary law (Simple Majority) to create or abolish — UPSC trap on two-stage process
Not a constitutional amendment under Article 368 — Parliament acts by ordinary legislation after state resolution
Only Vidhan Sabha resolution required — Vidhan Parishad (if existing) has no role in its own abolition

concepts.name: Majority in Rajya Sabha for Special Powers (Article 249 and 312)
key_dimensions: Article 249 (legislation on State List for national interest): 2/3rd of members present and voting in Rajya Sabha — Special Majority but only in Rajya Sabha
Article 312 (creation of All India Services): same — 2/3rd present and voting in Rajya Sabha only
UPSC trap: These are Special Majorities confined to Rajya Sabha — Lok Sabha has no role in passing the resolution
Duration of Article 249 resolution: one year, renewable — national interest legislation lapses after six months of resolution expiry

concepts.name: Majority for Vice President Election and Removal
key_dimensions: Election of Vice President (Article 66): by Electoral College of both Houses of Parliament — Simple Majority with single transferable vote
Removal (Article 67): resolution passed by Rajya Sabha by effective majority + agreed to by Lok Sabha by simple majority — UPSC trap: asymmetric majority requirement
14 days advance notice required for removal resolution
Vice President's electoral college excludes state legislatures — unlike President's election

concepts.name: Joint Sitting and Majority (Article 108)
key_dimensions: Joint sitting resolves deadlock on ordinary bills — Simple Majority of total members present and voting at joint sitting
NOT applicable to Money Bills, Constitution Amendment Bills, and Rajya Sabha exclusive bills — UPSC trap list
Presided over by Speaker of Lok Sabha — not the Vice President
Joint sitting has been held only once in Indian history (1961, Dowry Prohibition Bill) — factual anchor

concepts.name: Majority for Confidence Motion vs. No-Confidence Motion
key_dimensions: Both require Simple Majority of members present and voting in Lok Sabha
Confidence motion is moved by the government; No-confidence by opposition — procedural distinction
UPSC trap: There is no constitutional provision for confidence motion — it is a constitutional convention
Vote on account and budget defeat can also lead to resignation — implied no-confidence

concepts.name: Casting Vote and Tie-Breaking in Majorities
key_dimensions: Speaker/Chairman does not vote in the first instance but exercises casting vote in case of tie (Article 100)
Casting vote is not a 'majority' mechanism — it resolves equality, not determines majority
UPSC trap: In Rajya Sabha, Chairman (Vice President) also has casting vote — applies to both Houses
Presidential assent and majority: President cannot alter the majority verdict — must assent or return (except Money Bills)

concepts.name: Majority in State Legislature for Specific Decisions
key_dimensions: Ratification of constitutional amendments (Article 368 proviso): Simple Majority in state legislature
Passage of state bills: generally Simple Majority — UPSC trap: states cannot pass Special Majority laws independently for constitutional changes
Resolution for President's Rule revocation: not required from state legislature — Governor/President decides
Removal of state Legislative Assembly Speaker: Effective Majority — mirrors Union Parliament provision

concepts.name: Majority Traps: Overlapping and Confusing Provisions (Comparative Analysis)
key_dimensions: President removal (2/3rd of total) vs. Judge removal (2/3rd present and voting + majority of total) — critical distinction
Speaker removal (Special Majority) vs. Deputy Speaker removal (Effective Majority) — most common UPSC trap
National Emergency continuation (Special Majority) vs. President's Rule continuation (Simple Majority) — asymmetry
Article 368 Special Majority: 'present and voting' component + 'total membership' component must BOTH be met — can fail even with 2/3rd if quorum is low
